The Blind Men and the Elephant: Why Can Everyone Touch a Real Part and Still Go Wrong Together?
A king ordered the people in his city who had been blind from birth to be gathered.
He also had an elephant brought in.
One person was led to its head, another felt its ear, and others its tusk, trunk, body, leg, hindquarters, tail, or tuft of hair at the tail's end.
Each time, the person guiding them said:
“This is what an elephant is like.”
The king then came before them and asked:
“You have now seen the elephant. What is it like?”
The person who had touched its head said an elephant was like a jar.
The one who had touched its ear said it was like a winnowing basket.
The one who had touched its tusk said it was like a plowshare.
Others compared it to a granary, a pillar, a mortar, a pestle, or a broom.
Each insisted that what they had touched was the elephant.
They began contradicting one another and finally even striking one another with their fists.
The king watched, pleased.
Today, the story is often summarized as:
Everyone sees only part of the truth, so do not be stubborn. Bring different perspectives together.
The lesson is appealing.
Everyone in the story really has encountered part of the same elephant. They are not inventing things out of nothing or deliberately lying.
The leg really is like a pillar.
The ear can indeed resemble a winnowing basket.
The hair at the end of the tail can certainly suggest a broom.
The mistake is not that they have touched nothing.
It happens in a small expansion of the claim:

The part I touched is like a pillar.
Therefore, an elephant is a pillar.
The partial experience is true.
The conclusion about the whole exceeds what the experience can support.
But ending the essay here would still omit one of the story's most important parts.
These people are not moving freely around the elephant, exchanging observations, and checking again as needed.
Someone else arranges which part each can touch.
The guide not only takes them to different parts, but tells each:
“This is the elephant.”
They do not receive a careful explanation:
“What you are touching is part of the elephant.”
They receive a suggestion about the whole from the person controlling their access.
The king then asks for public answers and watches the fight.
He is no neutral bystander who happens on a disagreement and tries to help everyone understand the truth.
The conditions of disagreement were organized by his own command.
The story is therefore about more than individual humility.
It also invites us to ask:
Who decides what each person can encounter?
Who tells them that the part is the whole?
Who can change position, see the entire picture, or arrange a second examination?
And who enjoys watching them attack one another?
If we blame only the elephant's examiners for their “narrow outlook,” we remove the conditions of their knowledge from the story.
They certainly need to limit their conclusions.
But the king and those carrying out his orders cannot pretend the conflict arose only from the participants' stubborn characters.
Another boundary needs protecting here.
We cannot say, because everyone has touched a real part:
Every judgment about the elephant is equally correct.
“The elephant's leg is like a pillar” and “The entire elephant is a pillar” are not claims of equal strength.
The first compares one part.
The second substitutes the part for the whole.
Acknowledging a genuine basis in someone's experience does not mean accepting every conclusion they draw from it.
Likewise, different people having encountered something real does not mean that putting all their metaphors together automatically produces an elephant.
A jar, basket, plowshare, granary, pillar, mortar, pestle, and broom will not assemble themselves into a living animal.
Shared understanding also requires knowing:
That these parts belong to the same object.
That they occupy different positions.
How they connect.
How the object can act.
And where each comparison begins to fail.
Adding perspectives does not make the object appear.
“Everyone has their own truth” is therefore not the story's most defensible conclusion.
Everyone has their own point of contact.
Those positions yield different experiences.
But differing experiences do not make the elephant wholly a pillar, a granary, and a broom at the same time.
The object still constrains interpretation.
A fuller judgment does not mean everyone keeps their original conclusion and politely says, “You're right too.”
It means giving everyone a chance to revise:
What I touched really was like a pillar, but it was a leg.
What you touched really was like a basket, but it was an ear.
We need to learn more about how these parts belong to the same elephant.
Such revisions do not erase individual experience.
They return it to the scope it can actually sustain.
The story uses people blind from birth as its characters.
Retelling it publicly requires particular care.
Actual visual impairment does not naturally produce stubbornness, ignorance, or fighting.
Nor is the problem that these people are untrustworthy because of their bodily condition.
Each accurately encounters the object under the conditions they have been allowed.
The error arises through three things occurring together:
Access is limited.
The part is presented as the whole.
The participants then elevate their experience into an exclusive conclusion.
Blaming everything on “people who cannot see” overlooks the sighted king who deliberately arranged the conflict.
Why is the king pleased?
The text does not give a detailed account of his psychology.
We cannot casually invent a desire to show the absurdity of sectarian disputes, or a deliberate attempt to consolidate his rule through conflict.
But his pleasure in the fighting casts at least one further shadow:
Not everyone is eager to resolve every disagreement.
When people attack each other over the part they have encountered, whoever controls the overall arrangement may suffer no loss.
It may even make their position easier to maintain.
This does not mean every disagreement about knowledge has a manipulator behind it.
But when a dispute remains stuck, it reminds us to examine not only the disputants but whoever set the conditions of access:
Can each person obtain only different fragments?
Has the evidence been divided?
Can some people change position while others cannot?
Does someone keep demanding debate over conclusions while never allowing a shared approach to the object?
Conversely, not every dispute can be attributed to the design of the surroundings.
The people in the story really do strike one another.
Even without knowing they have touched only a part, they can still speak more cautiously:
“The elephant I encountered was like a pillar.”
Rather than:
“The elephant can only be a pillar. You are all wrong.”
Limited conditions of knowledge do not remove responsibility for the strength of one's conclusions.
We need not see everything before we are entitled to speak.
But when we know our contact is partial, our language should retain that boundary.
Between “what I know” and “how the whole thing is,” there needs to be a distance we do not rush to cross.
The story also shows that real shared understanding requires more than asking everyone to respect one another.
If the king still permits no movement and lets each person touch only one part, they may stop fighting without getting closer to the elephant.
Courtesy can protect communication.
It cannot replace fresh contact.
People need to return to the object:
Exchange positions.
Touch more parts.
Compare different descriptions.
Let original conclusions meet new experience.
Even acknowledge that helpful comparisons may still be insufficient to describe a whole that breathes, moves, and eats.
Shared understanding does not aim to preserve every viewpoint unchanged.
It aims to let viewpoints change before a shared object.
Everyone has touched a true part.
That statement matters because it keeps us from denying someone's entire experience merely because their overall judgment is wrong.
But it needs its other half:
A true part does not automatically become the whole truth simply by being true.
And when many people go wrong together, we cannot blame only each person's failure to see far enough.
Sometimes they have been placed where only partial contact is possible, and someone benefits from the resulting conflict between those parts.
So when a dispute involves real evidence on all sides, we can keep asking:
Are these pieces of evidence really describing the same object?
Which part does each cover?
Who has the chance to encounter more?
Who determined that the problem could be seen only this way?
Can we approach the object again, rather than merely state our existing conclusions more loudly?
The elephant is there all along.
What is missing is more than additional perspectives.
It is a path that lets people move from their own position and allows the object to change their judgment.

*Textual basis: the elephant parable in the Pali Udāna 6.4, the Tittha Sutta. In this version, a king orders people blind from birth to be assembled and assigned different parts of an elephant to touch. The guide tells each, “This is what an elephant is like.” They then elevate partial experience into judgments about the whole and begin fighting, to the king's satisfaction. This essay avoids equating actual visual impairment with ignorance, focusing instead on partial truth, inference about the whole, and arranged conditions of access.*
